summary: Follow-up after last week's incident where NorthStar saw a multi-minute longtail surge during peak fraud-detection window. Call reviewed mitigations, quick rollbacks, and proposed runbook and dedicated-burst pilot. Agreement to run deterministic replay and share sanitized logs; emphasis on KV cache warming, autoscaling thresholds, and audit/tech reviewer access.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-28 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Gupta (Redwood AE), Carlos Rios (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (NorthStar Head of ML), Mark D. Lee (NorthStar SRE), Jon Park (Eng Manager)

Summary (automated): brief incident recap, proposed pilot, technical actions for mitigating longtail and improving observability, scheduling of replay.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I know the last 48 hours have been rough. We wanted to move from triage into a concrete recovery velocity plan.
[00:14] Aisha: Yeah thanks, um, appreciate you fitting this in. We've still got higher-than-normal 95 and 99 pct tails and the fraud window yesterday basically amplified it.
[00:28] Carlos: quick clarification — when you say 99 pct tail, do you mean token tail or request latency?
[00:33] Mark: request latency, the entire inference call, so for some payloads it stretched to multiple minutes, not just a token hiccup.
[00:41] Jon: and to be clear, our users see a stuck timeout which then cascades to replay logic and duplicates requests.
[00:50] Maya: right. ok, so agenda is: brief recap, what we validated (KV cache cold-start patterns), what we propose (dedicated burst pilot + revised autoscale), and next steps.
[01:05] Aisha: quick thing — we already rotated to the fallback model last night which helped but the quality delta was too high for some flows.
[01:15] Carlos: yeah the fallback selection is conservative; we can tweak similarity thresholds so only lower-risk flows fall back.
[01:20] (crosstalk)
[01:30] Maya: Carlos, can you run through the kernel-level hypothesis? I know you found something about fragmented GPU queues.
[01:35] Carlos: sure — so from the traces you sent, we saw batches forming then one large long-running decode got scheduled onto the same CUDA stream and it blocked async eviction of KV pages, which effectively amplified wait for next requests. The runtime ought to isolate those heavy decodes into a separate queue or prefer early-preempt.
[01:58] Mark: is that the same as the K V cache eviction issue we saw a month back? transcripts kept saying K-V cache but sometimes SV cache, so just making sure.
[02:08] Carlos: similar but not identical — previously it was a memory leak during key-value cache compaction; this time it was scheduling + mixing short and very long sequences on the same worker.
[02:18] Aisha: we do have a bimodal sequence length distribution during fraud windows — long sequences for batch verification and many short ones for quick scoring.
[02:29] Maya: ok makes sense. so tactical: dedicated-burst pool where you can pin critical flows; and runtime tweaks: strict priority queues for short-seq scoring, plus pre-warm KV cache for known prefixes.
[02:42] Jon: about the pre-warm: how big is the warming window? we can't keep everything warm.
[02:46] Carlos: agreed; we recommend top-200 prefix tuples (based on your last 7 days) — it's a cost vs coverage tradeoff. We can give a suggested set after we run the sanitized prompt analysis.
[02:58] Aisha: that prompt analysis — we'll provide top-500 queries but need guidance on what to sanitize. Is there a tool you use?
[03:05] Maya: we have a scrub script and can take PII out; we'll also accept just hashing if you prefer. send it into the shared s3 and we'll run matching. Link: https://redwood.com/s/nsf-scrub (note: placeholder)
[03:20] (short pause)
[03:25] Mark: security checkpoint — we need to ensure logs we share are redacted and that any KMS keys are customer-managed when we test VPC peering.
[03:35] Maya: absolutely, we support customer-managed KMS and will use the private deployment plane for any sensitive exchanges. We'll attach the SOC2 docs in the thread.
[03:45] Jon: can you repeat the suggested autoscale thresholds? Yesterday the autoscaler reacted only after 30s of queue build-up.
[03:52] Carlos: since your median p95 is low but p99 high, we suggest a two-tier threshold: aggressive horizontal scale at small queue depth (3-5) for low-latency workers and a capacity ramp policy for long-run decodes so heavy jobs go to dedicated nodes.
[04:12] Aisha: ok, so separate node types for long-run jobs — does that require model replication?
[04:17] Carlos: yep, light replication for the scoring model on the tail nodes; model-sharing via the runtime keeps weights loaded so the delta is minimal.
[04:26] Maya: we also suggested a short-term mitigation: set fallback to earlier model snapshot with higher stability but slightly worse quality, and enable a suppressed retry policy to prevent duplicate spikes.
[04:40] Aisha: we tried snapshot-3 but some of the fraud heuristics drop, we need to test behavior against edge cases.
[04:47] Jon: what about the circuit-breaker you mentioned?
[04:50] Carlos: the circuit-breaker is token-based: if a single request consumes > X seconds of GPU time we either preempt it or route subsequent similar requests to fallback until the spike subsides. It's aggressive but stops cascade.
[05:05] (background noise)
[05:12] Mark: last incident timeline — can we confirm the exact window we should replay? We want to make the replay deterministic.
[05:18] Maya: you gave traces covering 14:52-15:08 UTC yesterday?
[05:22] Mark: yes that's the main window; there was also a smaller blip at 16:40 but primary is the earlier one.
[05:30] Carlos: for deterministic replay we need: sanitized request bodies, the model version and kv-cache seed, and exact sequence lengths. The KV cache seed is important; without it replay won't surface the scheduling contention.
[05:45] Aisha: how do we export KV seeds? we don't want to export secrets.
[05:50] Carlos: we can export a hash/offset map instead, which you can cross-check; Redwood won't store the raw seeds. We'll document the flow.
[06:02] Maya: ok on that privacy approach. Next — pricing for dedicated-burst pilot: Maya?
[06:06] Maya: we'll propose a 30-day pilot: reserved nodes + burst capacity with a soft cap, and a refund if we don't meet 95 pct tail target improvement. I'll send numbers in the follow-up.
[06:18] Mark: refund? I like the idea of a performance SLA for the pilot.
[06:22] Maya: it's conditional on running the replay and following the pre-warm recipe.
[06:28] Jon: technical question — if we do VPC peering test, do you need inbound ports open?
[06:33] Carlos: we ask for a single egress rule and a shared peering in the same region; we'll run perf harness over HTTPS with mutual TLS. No inbound holes into your subnet.
[06:44] Aisha: about observability — we need per-request token-level timing, not just aggregated percentiles. Is that feasible with your current console?
[06:53] Carlos: yes, we can give a per-route trace and token timing breakdown, though retention beyond 30 days is an add-on.
[07:02] Maya: and we can add custom dashboards for your fraud flow IDs so you can see hot sequences.
[07:09] (brief hold)
[07:18] Mark: we've had internal discussion about fail-open vs fail-closed. Last night we failed-open to preserve throughput but exposed downstream fraud risk.
[07:28] Aisha: yep, we prefer fail-closed for scoring that triggers enforcement, but for non-blocking alerts fail-open is ok. We need clearer mapping by flow.
[07:38] Maya: agree — part of the pilot is classification of flows into critical enforcement vs informational; critical ones go to dedicated pool with stricter SLAs.
[07:48] Jon: what about telemetry overhead? if we enable token timing per request that could increase overhead.
[07:54] Carlos: minimal — the runtime samples token timing for a subset and provides full traces for flagged requests; we can tune sample rate.
[08:02] Aisha: can we see a sample of the sanitized trace output? small excerpt?
[08:07] Carlos: yes I'll paste an example in the follow-up thread — shows seq len, token timing, GPU wait and queue deltas.
[08:15] Maya: ok, moving to schedule — Carlos will run the replay on a dedicated pool and share results within 7 business days, correct?
[08:21] Carlos: correct. I'll need the sanitized payloads and the model/version.
[08:25] Aisha: we'll get that in by Friday.
[08:28] (pause)
[08:35] Mark: small ask — can Redwood also run a synthetic burst test with mixed seq lengths to validate the priority queues?
[08:41] Carlos: yes that's part of the regression run; we'll simulate your bimodal traffic and show before/after tail curves.
[08:49] Maya: action recap: Redwood shares security docs and pricing; NorthStar shares sanitized traces and enables peering test window; Redwood runs replay + mixed-seq synthetic and returns results. Do we all agree?
[08:59] All: yes / yep / agreed.
[09:05] Jon: one last thing — we might want to invite our infra director to the follow-up if the replay shows infra-level work.
[09:12] Maya: please do; the more stakeholders the better.
[09:18] Aisha: ok thanks everyone, we'll be in touch.
